title: Short Stuff: Poe Toaster
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Poe Toaster, the mysterious figure who visited Edgar Allan Poe's grave in Baltimore's Westminster Burying Ground on or around Poe's January 19 birthday for decades, toasting with cognac and leaving three roses. The hosts cover Poe's burial history and the 1875 monument and exhumation, the origin of the ritual around the 1949 centennial, the cognac and rose traditions, the claim by former ad executive Sam Porpora in 2007 to be the toaster, historian Jeff Jerome's role, the notes left behind (including the "torch will be passed" note and a Super Bowl prediction), the tradition ending around 2012, and the later 2016 public audition of new Poe Toasters at a party with apple cider.

segments.title: Opening banter and Halloween setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the Short Stuff episode on the Poe Toaster, framing it as a spooky October topic and setting up Poe's mysterious grave visitor.

segments.title: Poe's burial and grave monument
segments.summary: Poe died at 40 in 1849 and was buried in Westminster Burying Ground in Baltimore, initially in an unmarked grave. Local academics raised money for a monument, and in 1875 he was moved to a better site. About ten years later his wife and mother-in-law were buried with him.

segments.title: Origins of the Poe Toaster ritual
segments.summary: Starting around 1949, the centennial of Poe's death, a mysterious man dressed in black with a white scarf and wide-brimmed hat began visiting the grave on Poe's birthday, January 19, usually between midnight and 6 am. He toasted Poe with cognac and left three red roses, which the hosts say are likely a tribute to Poe, his wife Virginia, and his mother-in-law Maria.

segments.title: Sam Porpora's claim and Jeff Jerome's skepticism
segments.summary: In 2007, 92-year-old former ad executive Sam Porpora claimed to be the Poe Toaster, saying he did it in 1960 as a publicity stunt to raise money for the run-down church. Poe Museum curator Jeff Jerome, considered the de facto historian of the toaster, doubts the claim and says he has no idea who the real toaster was. He says he had a signal arrangement with the toaster to confirm authenticity. The hosts note Porpora gave no clear reason for coming forward late in life.

segments.title: Notes, sons theory, and the tradition ending
segments.summary: The toaster left notes, including one saying the torch would be passed and another saying the toaster had died. Jeff Jerome believes the torch passed to the toaster's sons, who were lax in their efforts, with one note predicting a 2001 Super Bowl upset. The visits stopped around 2012 and Jerome declared the tradition over.

segments.title: Poe Toaster auditions and closing thoughts
segments.summary: In 2016 the Poe Museum held a public party and audition for new Poe Toasters, with a raffle, a Poe-themed cake, and apple cider toasts during the daytime. The hosts say they wish the tradition had been left alone, though they like the idea of honoring Poe. They joke about auditioning themselves.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up, say they hope the Poe Toaster's identity is never revealed, and close with the Short Stuff sign-off and a note about the show's production company and podcast apps.
